title: The elephant in the dark
hook: people touch an elephant in a dark room and call it a fan, a pillar, a throne (Rumi, Masnavi 3.1259ff)
tomorrow: Abba Moses and the leaking basket

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabia's torch and bucket: fire for paradise, water for hell, and love for God alone. Your line was for its own sake. Did one kind thing go unannounced? Day seventy-two.

Think of a family argument about something that happened years ago. Your sister remembers one thing. Your dad remembers another. You remember a third, and you'd swear to it. Everyone was there. Everyone is sure. And somehow nobody's lying. Each of you touched a different part of the same afternoon. The Persian poet Rumi, writing in the twelve hundreds, told a story about exactly this, set in a dark room, with a very large visitor inside. Today's story is the elephant in the dark.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE.` → `EVERYONE IS SURE.` → `A DARK ROOM, A LARGE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: Rumi tells it in his long poem, the Masnavi, in its third book. Some travelers bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one, and they keep it in a dark house. People crowd in to see it. But it's too dark to see anything, so each one reaches out and touches. One hand finds the trunk: this creature, he says, is like a water pipe. Another finds the ear: no, it's like a fan. Another wraps her arms around a leg: it's a pillar. Another pats the back: it's shaped like a throne. Each description is honest. Each is about something real. And each is wrong about the whole. Then Rumi gives the line the story turns on. If each of them had held a candle, he says, the difference would have gone out of their words. Nobody needed to shout louder. They needed light. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and Sufi teacher, and in the poem he uses the story to say something about the limits of our senses: the hand can only know what it touches. Readers have taken it in many directions since, and people disagree about how far to push it. An older cousin of the story appears in the Buddhist Udana, where a king has blind men describe an elephant, and they end up in a fistfight. So the picture has traveled. Here's where it lands on an ordinary day. When someone describes something completely differently from you, it's possible one of you is simply wrong. But it's also possible you've got the ear, and they've got the leg. Before arguing, bring a candle: ask what their hand is touching.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.` · `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `WITH A CANDLE, NO DIFFERENCE.` · `ASK WHAT THEIR HAND IS TOUCHING.` · then, large: `BRING A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one person how they see something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who sees some matter differently from you. Not the biggest fight you have; something small and real. Picture the two of you in the dark room, each with a hand on the elephant. Ask yourself, gently: what part might they be touching that I'm not? Then think of one honest question you could ask them today, a question that begins with how do you see it. Just picture asking. The bell holds the time.
Masnavi. Rumi's long poem, where hands in a dark room each touch an elephant, each honest, each partial, until a candle could have ended the argument.
Your line: bring a candle. Today, when someone sees it differently, ask one question before you argue: what are you touching that I'm not? Day seventy-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Rumi's Masnavi often tell the elephant in the dark when talking about the limits of what any one person perceives, and teachers in many settings use it to open conversations across disagreement.

match.prompt: which hand found what — tap the pairs.

myth: each person in the dark room was lying
each described something real. each was wrong only about the whole.
an older version appears in a Buddhist text
the Udana has a king ask blind men to describe an elephant.
Rumi's answer is that they should argue louder
if each had held a candle, he says, the difference would have gone out of their words.

fork.setup: you're in the dark house. you've touched the elephant's ear, and it's plainly a fan. your neighbor insists it's a pillar. what does Rumi say would settle it?
options: whoever touched it first is right
a vote of everyone in the room
fork.reveal: a candle. with light, he says, the difference would have gone out of their words. each hand was honest; none could see the whole.

original.note: Persian: elephant. Rumi wrote the Masnavi in Persian, and the story's heading speaks of an elephant in a dark house.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about blind men and an elephant.
what it means: every hand in the dark is honest and partial; light, not louder argument, ends the dispute.
what a scholar hears: Rumi's version (Masnavi 3) follows the poet Sanai's, and an older form appears in the Buddhist Udana.

notes: Masnavi 3.1259ff paraphrased (Nicholson's full Masnavi translation dates from 1925–40 and is not on the public-domain list; Whinfield 1898 abridges it). Confirm the four comparisons (water pipe, fan, pillar, throne) and the candle line.
Rumi's own framing concerns the limits of sense perception; the script says readers have taken it further and disagree how far. Please confirm this is fairly put.
Udana 6.4 (the king, the blind men and the elephant, ending in a quarrel): confirm reference. Sanai's earlier version (Hadiqat al-Haqiqa): confirm.
Persian پیل (pil) for elephant, and that the heading reads pil andar khana-yi tarik: confirm.
